items.topic: Walker ambulation — all tips/wheels on ground; step with weak/injured leg first
items.stem: The nurse teaches a client recovering from right hip surgery to use a pickup walker. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: Move the walker forward, ensure all four tips or wheels are on the ground, then step with the weaker (surgical) leg first, followed by the stronger leg
Step with the stronger leg first while lifting two walker tips off the floor
Pull up from the chair by tipping the walker toward you
Look continuously at your feet while leaning far over the front bar

rationales.A: Correct. MedlinePlus: all 4 tips/wheels on ground before stepping; step with weak/surgical leg first, then the other. AAOS: position walker with all four legs on even ground; move injured leg into walker first.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Weight should not be placed until all tips/wheels are down; weak/injured leg steps first for typical weight-bearing walker gait.
rationales.C: Incorrect. MedlinePlus: do not pull on or tilt the walker to stand; use chair armrests.
rationales.D: Incorrect. MedlinePlus/AAOS: look forward, not down at feet; keep toes inside the walker frame.

items.topic: Compression stockings — apply in morning before out of bed; smooth wrinkles/bunching
items.stem: The nurse teaches a postoperative client about graduated compression stockings. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: Put the stockings on first thing in the morning before getting out of bed, and smooth out wrinkles so they do not bunch
Wait until evening when legs are most swollen before applying the stockings
Roll or fold the tops of the stockings down to create a tighter cuff
Apply only one stocking on the unaffected leg

rationales.A: Correct. MedlinePlus: put on first thing in the morning before out of bed; smooth wrinkles; do not let stockings bunch. Cleveland Clinic: smooth out rolls; avoid bunching.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Morning application is preferred because legs have least swelling then.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Cleveland Clinic: never turn tops over — tourniquet-like effect. MedlinePlus: avoid bunching/wrinkles.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Stockings are applied as prescribed, typically to both legs when ordered for DVT risk/venous support.

items.topic: Denture care — remove overnight; store in water or denture-soaking solution
items.stem: The nurse teaches an older adult about removable denture care. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: Take dentures out overnight and place them in water or a mild denture-soaking solution
Leave dentures in continuously day and night without removal
Scrub dentures vigorously with whitening toothpaste and a stiff brush
Soak metal-attachment dentures in undiluted household bleach overnight

rationales.A: Correct. MedlinePlus Dentures/Denture problems: take out at night; store in water or denture-cleansing liquid. Mayo Clinic: soak overnight in water or mild soaking solution.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Overnight removal helps prevent sores/inflammation and keeps dentures moist when stored properly.
rationales.C: Incorrect. MedlinePlus: do not clean with toothpaste; Mayo: avoid harsh/abrasive toothpaste and stiff brushes.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Mayo: avoid bleach products that can weaken dentures; chlorine solutions can damage metal attachments.

items.topic: Hearing aid care — protect from heat/moisture; turn off when not in use; avoid hairspray while worn
items.stem: The nurse reinforces hearing-aid care teaching for a client. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: Keep hearing aids away from heat and moisture, turn them off when not in use, and avoid hairspray while wearing them
Rinse hearing aids under running water each night and dry with a hair dryer on high heat
Leave hearing aids powered on continuously, including overnight storage
Apply hairspray freely while the aids are in place to protect electronics

rationales.A: Correct. FDA and NIDCD: keep away from heat/moisture; turn off when not in use; avoid hairspray/hair products while wearing. FDA also advises against water on aids.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Water and high heat damage electronics; FDA specifically warns against water and hair dryers.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Turn aids off when not in use.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Avoid hairspray and hair-care products while wearing aids.

items.topic: Indwelling catheter drainage — keep bag below bladder; do not rest bag on floor
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: A client has an indwelling urinary catheter. Which nursing action best supports infection prevention during maintenance?

options.text: Keep the collecting bag below the level of the bladder at all times and do not rest the bag on the floor
Hang the drainage bag above bladder level to improve gravity flow into the bladder
Place the drainage bag on the floor beside the bed for stability
Raise the bag above the bladder when transferring so tubing stays taut

rationales.A: Correct. CDC CAUTI guideline: keep collecting bag below bladder at all times; do not rest bag on floor. MedlinePlus: bag always lower than bladder; do not place bag on floor.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Bag above bladder risks backflow of urine into the bladder.
rationales.C: Incorrect. CDC/MedlinePlus: do not place/rest bag on the floor.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Raising bag above bladder promotes reflux and contamination risk.

items.topic: Safe injection — one needle, one syringe, only one time (even if needle changed)
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: Which practice meets CDC safe injection recommendations?

options.text: Use a new sterile needle and syringe for each patient — do not reuse a syringe on another patient even if the needle is changed
Change only the needle and reuse the same syringe for the next patient
Draw medication for several patients from one syringe by changing needles between patients
Access a multidose vial with a syringe that was already used on a patient, then use that vial for others

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: One Needle, One Syringe, Only One Time; do not administer from the same syringe to multiple patients even if the needle is changed.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Changing the needle does not make a used syringe safe for another patient.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Syringes are single-use; reuse between patients transmits infection.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CDC: do not enter a medication vial with a syringe/needle used on a patient for subsequent patients.

items.topic: PTSD flashback — ground in present (senses/here-and-now); reassure safety
items.stem: A client with PTSD suddenly appears terrified, stares past the nurse, and seems to be re-experiencing a past assault. Which nursing action is the priority?

options.text: Calmly orient the client to the present using grounding (e.g., what they can see/hear/touch now) and reassure that they are safe
Insist the client immediately recount every detail of the trauma aloud
Leave the client alone in a dark room until the episode ends
Argue that the trauma never happened and demand they 'snap out of it'

rationales.A: Correct. NHSGGC: grounding pulls attention back to here-and-now during flashbacks (senses). VA Stress First Aid: orient to present; describe surroundings/non-distressing sensory details; slow breathing as needed.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Forcing detailed trauma recounting during an acute flashback is not first-line acute grounding care.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Leaving an acutely distressed/disoriented client alone is unsafe.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Arguing/denying experience is nontherapeutic and escalating.

items.topic: NGN bowtie — PTSD flashback recognition; grounding/safety actions; monitor orientation/distress
items.stem: A veteran suddenly crouches, hyperventilates, and shouts as if under attack after a door slam, then does not respond to ordinary questions. Complete the bowtie: the priority condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.

actions.text: Orient to the present with grounding (safe place; name what is seen/heard/touched now)
Leave the client alone immediately to 'work it out'
Speak calmly; coach slow breathing while staying with the client
Force the client to describe the combat event in full detail right now
Apply physical restraints as first-line for flashbacks

parameters.text: Orientation to person/place/time and connection to the present
Level of distress, breathing pattern, and safety risk

rationales.K1: Incorrect. No cue pattern pointing primarily to hypoglycemia.
rationales.K2: Correct. Sudden re-experiencing after a trigger with loss of ordinary responsiveness fits PTSD flashback/intrusion.
rationales.K3: Incorrect. No opioid toxicity pattern (e.g., pinpoint pupils, apnea) described.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Vertigo alone does not explain trauma-triggered panic behaviours.
rationales.A1: Correct. Grounding/present orientation is first-line for flashbacks (NHSGGC/VA).
rationales.A2: Incorrect. Do not leave an acutely distressed/disoriented client alone.
rationales.A3: Correct. Calm presence and slow breathing support SFA calming/orientation.
rationales.A4: Incorrect. Forced trauma narrative mid-flashback is not acute grounding care.
rationales.A5: Incorrect. Restraints are not first-line for flashbacks.
rationales.P1: Correct. Monitor return of orientation/present awareness.
rationales.P2: Correct. Monitor distress, breathing, and safety.
rationales.P3: Incorrect. Not relevant to acute flashback response.

items.jurisdiction_note: Fixing Long-Term Care Act, 2021 mandatory reporting duties for LTC staff/regulated health professionals; CNO Accountability to report FAQ.
items.topic: Ontario LTC — nurse must report suspected resident abuse/neglect (FLTCA / CNO)
items.stem: An Ontario RN working in a long-term care home has reasonable grounds to suspect that a resident was abused by a staff member and that the resident was harmed. Which action meets legal and professional accountabilities?

options.text: Immediately report the suspicion through the required LTC reporting pathway (to the Director / designated reporting line) — confidentiality does not excuse failing to report
Wait several weeks to see whether the resident complains formally before taking any action
Keep the information confidential and tell no one because of PHIPA
Confront the alleged abuser privately and close the matter without any report

rationales.A: Correct. CNO: FLTCA requires nurses to report improper/incompetent care or abuse resulting in harm or risk of harm. Steps to Justice: LTC workers/regulated health professionals must report suspected abuse/neglect; duty applies even if information would otherwise be confidential.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Reporting is required when there are reasonable grounds to suspect; delaying undermines resident protection.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Mandatory reporting duties override ordinary confidentiality in this setting.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Informal confrontation without required reporting does not meet FLTCA/CNO accountabilities.
